title: Adjectives and agreement

objectives.can: Match an adjective to its noun in case, number and gender, in attributive and predicate position.

explanation.summary: An adjective describes a noun, and in Greek it matches the noun in case, number and gender. Its position, with or without the article, tells you whether it says 'the good man' or 'the man is good'.

sections.heading: Agreement
body: An English adjective never changes: 'good' stays 'good' with every noun. A Greek adjective takes the case, number and gender of the noun it belongs to. In Matthew 12:35, ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος has three words in the nominative singular masculine; ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ has three in the genitive singular masculine.

Most adjectives are made of the endings you already know. The masculine and neuter use second-declension endings (-ος, -ον) and the feminine uses first-declension endings (-η or -α). Such an adjective is listed under the masculine nominative singular: ἀγαθός, καλός, πιστός. Its three forms are ἀγαθός, ἀγαθή, ἀγαθόν. The paradigms below are filled in from the texts.

Agreement is in case, number and gender, but not in declension. A masculine noun of the first declension, such as μαθητής, takes the masculine endings of the adjective, which look like second-declension endings. The gender and number of the noun decide which column of the adjective is used.

sections.heading: Attributive position: 'the good man'
body: An adjective is attributive when it is part of the description of the noun, like 'good' in 'the good shepherd'. With the article, Greek has two ways to write this. The adjective stands between the article and the noun (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος), or it follows the noun and repeats the article (ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός, as in John 10:11). Both mean the same thing: 'the good man', 'the good shepherd'. There may be a slight difference in emphasis, which is a matter of style.
The key point is that the adjective is joined to the article of its noun, either directly or by a second article.

sections.heading: Predicate position: 'the man is good'
body: An adjective is a predicate when it says something about the noun. It is not tied to the article: it stands outside the article–noun group. In Romans 7:12, ὁ νόμος ἅγιος means 'the law is holy'. There is no verb, because εἰμί is often left out; Greek simply puts the two words side by side. In 1 Corinthians 1:9, πιστὸς ὁ θεός stands in the same way, with the adjective first.

So the rule of thumb is: article–adjective–noun, or article–noun–article–adjective, is attributive; adjective–article–noun, or article–noun–adjective with no second article, is predicate. When there is no article at all, as in πᾶν κτίσμα θεοῦ καλόν in 1 Timothy 4:4, you have to use the sense and a verb that may be understood: 'every creature of God is good'. This is a strong tendency, not an exceptionless law.

sections.heading: Adjectives standing alone, and adjectives with two endings
body: A Greek adjective can do the work of a noun. In Matthew 5:45, πονηροὺς καὶ ἀγαθούς are 'evil people and good people'. The article often goes with it: the masculine for 'the good man' or 'the good people', the neuter for 'the good thing' or 'good things'.

A few adjectives have only two sets of endings, because the masculine and the feminine are alike. αἰώνιος, 'lasting, eternal', is the commonest. Its masculine and feminine forms are the same, and its neuter is αἰώνιον. The paradigm below shows this: the masculine and feminine columns are identical.

misunderstandings: The adjective does not have to be next to its noun, and it is not always the same declension as its noun. What must match is case, number and gender.
A final -ος on an adjective is not always masculine: with a few adjectives, such as αἰώνιος, the same form also serves for the feminine.

Dropping the article does not turn an adjective into a predicate by itself. When the noun has no article, the position rule cannot help, and you have to judge from the sense and from whether a verb is present or understood.
Words that English renders with 'other', 'first' or 'only' (ἄλλος, πρῶτος, μόνος) are still Greek adjectives and still agree with the noun they go with.

deeper.heading: Adjectives such as ἴδιος and μόνος
body: Some adjectives, such as ἴδιος ('one's own') and μόνος ('alone, only'), are often translated into English by an adverb or a possessive. They still agree with the noun or pronoun they describe, so the form tells you whom they refer to.
